job.style: a description of a classroom activity or experiment and what it shows

passage: In our Social Science class, we conducted a simulation to understand consumer protection. We analyzed four different scenarios involving market transactions. First, a high-profile executive purchased a luxury electronic device from a premium showroom, only to find it was defective and dangerous to use. This proved that exploitation is not limited to the poor or uneducated; anyone can be a victim of unfair trade practices. Second, we examined a packet of spices sold in a fancy, branded retail store that contained harmful additives, demonstrating that even expensive brands can sell adulterated goods. Third, we looked at a local food manufacturer who used an ISI mark on their spices instead of the required Agmark, highlighting that certification marks are specific to product categories. Finally, we studied the Consumer Protection Act (COPRA), which established a three-tier quasi-judicial machinery. We learned that a consumer does not need to approach the Supreme Court for every issue; instead, they can file complaints at the District, State, or National level depending on the value of the claim. This activity clarified that consumer rights are universal protections designed to ensure safety, information, and fair redressal for every citizen regardless of their social status or the prestige of the shop where they choose to shop.

items.evidence: This proved that exploitation is not limited to the poor or uneducated; anyone can be a victim of unfair trade practices.
items.q: A top executive bought a dangerous, faulty device. What did this case prove?
options: Anyone can be cheated, whatever their status
Only the poor and uneducated get cheated
Big showrooms always sell safe, sound goods
Safety rights cover food, not electronic goods
items.explain: Even a rich executive got a dangerous device, so exploitation is not limited to the poor.

wrong.why: thinks only poor or uneducated people are exploited
thinks premium shops cannot sell bad goods
thinks the right to safety covers only food

items.evidence: Second, we examined a packet of spices sold in a fancy, branded retail store that contained harmful additives, demonstrating that even expensive brands can sell adulterated goods.
items.q: Meena trusts only fancy branded stores for spices. What does the spice packet example show?
options: Even costly brands can sell impure goods
Branded retail stores cannot sell adulterated goods
Only poor buyers get spices with additives
Pure spices always carry an ISI mark
items.explain: The branded store's spices had harmful additives, so even expensive brands can sell adulterated goods.

wrong.why: thinks branded shops cannot sell adulterated goods
thinks only poor people are cheated
thinks ISI is the mark for food items

items.evidence: Third, we looked at a local food manufacturer who used an ISI mark on their spices instead of the required Agmark, highlighting that certification marks are specific to product categories.
items.q: Which mark should the local food maker have put on its spice packets, and why?
options: Used Agmark, as marks suit product types
Used ISI, as it is meant for food
Used ISI, as Agmark is for machines
Used any mark, as all marks are equal
items.explain: Spices need Agmark; certification marks are specific to product categories, so ISI was wrong.

wrong.why: thinks ISI mark is only for food items
swaps the roles of Agmark and ISI
over-generalises that any certification mark will do

items.evidence: We learned that a consumer does not need to approach the Supreme Court for every issue; instead, they can file complaints at the District, State, or National level depending on the value of the claim.
items.q: Under COPRA, what decides where a consumer complaint is filed?
options: The amount of money being claimed
The Supreme Court's choice for each case
The fee paid to a hired lawyer
The buyer's social status and education
items.explain: Complaints go to District, State or National level depending on the claim's value.

wrong.why: thinks every complaint goes to the Supreme Court
thinks a costly lawyer is needed to file a case
thinks status decides who gets protection

items.evidence: This activity clarified that consumer rights are universal protections designed to ensure safety, information, and fair redressal for every citizen regardless of their social status or the prestige of the shop where they choose to shop.
items.q: A poor farmer buys a faulty gas cylinder from a small village shop. Do consumer rights protect this buyer?
options: Yes, rights cover every citizen and shop
Yes, but only for food, not cylinders
No, rights depend on the shop's prestige
No, only educated buyers can claim them
items.explain: Consumer rights are universal, protecting every citizen whatever their social status or the shop's prestige.

wrong.why: thinks the right to safety covers only food
links protection to how fancy the shop is
thinks status decides who is protected
